subtopic_detail: Sequencing imaging before tissue sampling of an abdominal mass in a preschool child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional hospital. A 3-year-old girl is referred by her general practitioner, who felt a smooth lump on the left side of her tummy while examining her for a cough that has since resolved.

Her mother first noticed the lump while bathing her about 2 weeks ago and thought it was a full tummy. The girl has been eating normally, her energy is unchanged, and she has had no fevers, no bone pain, no bruising and no weight loss. She has never had a urinary tract infection.

On examination there is a smooth firm mass in the left upper abdomen that does not cross the midline. She is not pale and there is no lymphadenopathy, no periorbital bruising and no hepatomegaly. Her blood pressure is above the 95th centile for her age and height. Urine dipstick shows blood one plus with no protein, nitrites or leucocytes.

The general practitioner has already booked a computed tomography scan and a percutaneous core biopsy at a private radiology practice for next week.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Smooth firm left upper abdominal mass not crossing the midline, no lymphadenopathy, no periorbital bruising, no hepatomegaly, not pale
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (110-140), platelets 288 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), lactate dehydrogenase within normal limits, urine dipstick blood one plus with no protein nitrites or leucocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed with the planned computed tomography scan and percutaneous core biopsy next week
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of a renal tumour spills tumour cells into the retroperitoneum and upstages the disease to stage III under Children's Oncology Group criteria, committing the child to abdominal radiotherapy she might otherwise avoid. The scheduling outside a paediatric oncology centre compounds the error. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

options.text: Request a bone marrow aspirate and trephine with urinary catecholamine measurement
options.rationale: Marrow sampling and catecholamines are the right workup for a neuroblastoma, which typically crosses the midline and is accompanied by bone pain, periorbital bruising or marrow failure; none of those is present and a mass confined to one flank points elsewhere. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

options.text: Start an antihypertensive agent and review her blood pressure and abdomen in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Treating the hypertension in isolation ignores its cause, which in a child with a renal mass is usually renin secretion by the tumour or renal artery compression, and a 2-week delay is unjustifiable for an undiagnosed abdominal mass. (Source: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Abdominal mass

options.text: Arrange urgent abdominal ultrasound with Doppler of the renal vein and inferior vena cava
options.rationale: Ultrasound with Doppler is the correct first imaging step because it establishes the renal origin of the mass and, critically, looks for tumour thrombus extending into the renal vein and inferior vena cava, which changes the surgical approach and must be known before any operation. Referral to a paediatric oncology centre follows immediately, and tissue diagnosis is made by the treating surgical team rather than by percutaneous biopsy. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance
RCH CPG: Abdominal mass

options.text: Arrange contrast computed tomography of the chest and abdomen as the first imaging study
options.rationale: Cross-sectional chest and abdominal imaging is needed for staging, but it follows ultrasound rather than replacing it, and it neither answers the venous thrombus question as reliably nor avoids the radiation burden in a preschool child when the first question is simply whether the mass is renal. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

explanation.summary: An abdominal mass in a preschool child is a malignancy until proven otherwise, and the two dominant diagnoses are nephroblastoma and neuroblastoma. Distinguishing them at the bedside rests on whether the mass crosses the midline, whether the child looks systemically well, and whether there are marrow or bone features. Hypertension and haematuria point towards a renal origin. The management pathway diverges sharply from adult oncology practice in one respect: percutaneous biopsy of a suspected nephroblastoma is avoided because tumour spill upstages the disease and adds radiotherapy to the treatment. North American and European protocols differ, with upfront nephrectomy favoured in one and preoperative chemotherapy in the other, and Australian centres follow a defined protocol, which is another reason the child must reach a paediatric oncology centre before anyone takes tissue.
key_points: Ultrasound with Doppler of the renal vein and inferior vena cava is the first imaging study for a suspected renal tumour
Percutaneous biopsy upstages nephroblastoma through tumour spill and should not be arranged outside a paediatric oncology centre
A mass that crosses the midline in an unwell child with bone pain or periorbital bruising suggests neuroblastoma instead
Hypertension with haematuria in a child with a flank mass points to a renal origin
Refer immediately to a paediatric oncology centre, which coordinates staging imaging and definitive tissue diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Tumour thrombus reaches the inferior vena cava in around 4 to 10 per cent of nephroblastomas and occasionally extends to the right atrium; finding it before surgery is what changes the operative plan and the need for cardiac bypass.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Children's Haematology and Oncology Group: Renal tumour guidance

subtopic_detail: Escalating airway management when prone positioning fails in a newborn with a cleft soft palate
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a baby boy on the special care nursery at 36 hours of age. He was born at term and a cleft of the soft palate was noted on the newborn examination, along with a small receding chin.

He has been nursed prone since birth because of noisy breathing when supine. Overnight the nursing staff documented three desaturations to 78 per cent during sleep, each lasting about 20 seconds and settling with repositioning, and one further desaturation during a bottle feed with a soft teat.

He has lost 4 per cent of his birth weight. While you examine him he is awake and prone with oxygen saturations of 96 per cent in air, and his work of breathing at rest looks comfortable. A capillary blood gas taken at 6 am shows a pH of 7.30 with a partial pressure of carbon dioxide of 58 mmHg and a bicarbonate of 27 mmol/L. The nearest craniofacial service is in the tertiary centre 90 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152/min, blood pressure 64/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 48/min, SpO2 96% on room air while prone and awake, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Cleft of the soft palate, receding chin, comfortable work of breathing at rest while prone
data_table.Investigations: Capillary blood gas pH 7.30 (7.32-7.42), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 58 mmHg (35-45), bicarbonate 27 mmol/L (22-28)
data_table.Overnight observations: Three sleep desaturations to 78% lasting about 20 seconds, one desaturation during a bottle feed, weight loss 4% of birth weight

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue prone nursing and review him again after a further 24 hours of observation
options.rationale: Prone positioning is the correct first measure but it has now been tried and has failed, as shown by repeated sleep desaturations and a rising carbon dioxide while already prone; continuing it accepts ongoing intermittent hypoxaemia. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence

options.text: Insert a nasopharyngeal airway and continue oximetry while arranging craniofacial review
options.rationale: A nasopharyngeal airway stents the airway past the tongue base and is the standard next step in the Australian escalation ladder when positioning alone fails, and it can be managed in a special care nursery and maintained during transfer. The mildly raised carbon dioxide with a normal bicarbonate indicates obstruction that is real but not yet chronic, which is the window in which a nasopharyngeal airway works well. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence
Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources

options.text: Intubate him electively and transfer him ventilated to the tertiary neonatal intensive care unit
options.rationale: Intubation in this anatomy is technically difficult and commits an otherwise stable baby to sedation, ventilation and its complications, when a less invasive measure has not yet been tried. It becomes the right answer only if a nasopharyngeal airway fails or the baby develops respiratory failure. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence

options.text: Start nasogastric feeds to reduce the feeding desaturations and continue prone nursing
options.rationale: Nasogastric feeding addresses the feeding-related events and the weight loss, and will very likely be needed, but it leaves the sleep obstruction untreated and is therefore an incomplete answer to a problem that is primarily one of airway patency. (Source: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Pierre Robin sequence

options.text: Refer directly for mandibular distraction osteogenesis as definitive management of the obstruction
options.rationale: Mandibular distraction is a surgical option for babies who fail non-surgical airway measures, so it sits several rungs further up the ladder and is decided by the craniofacial team after a sleep study, not selected at 36 hours of age. (Source: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources)
source_refs: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources

explanation.summary: A receding chin with a cleft of the soft palate in a newborn with airway obstruction describes Pierre Robin sequence, in which a small mandible displaces the tongue base backwards and obstructs the pharynx. Management follows a stepwise ladder: prone or side positioning first, then a nasopharyngeal airway, then continuous positive airway pressure or tongue-lip adhesion, then mandibular distraction osteogenesis, with tracheostomy reserved for failure of all of these. Feeding difficulty runs alongside the airway problem because the cleft prevents an effective seal, and specialised soft compressible bottles with assisted delivery, or nasogastric supplementation, are commonly required. Objective assessment with overnight oximetry or polysomnography guides escalation better than daytime observation, since obstruction is worst during sleep. About half of affected babies have an associated syndrome, most often Stickler syndrome, so genetic and ophthalmological review is arranged.
key_points: The escalation ladder runs positioning, then nasopharyngeal airway, then continuous positive airway pressure or tongue-lip adhesion, then mandibular distraction, with tracheostomy last
Failure of positioning is defined by ongoing sleep desaturation or rising carbon dioxide while already prone
Sleep is when obstruction is worst, so overnight oximetry or polysomnography guides escalation, not daytime observation
Feeding support with specialised teats or nasogastric supplementation addresses the separate problem of poor seal across the cleft
Around half have an associated syndrome, most commonly Stickler syndrome, warranting genetics and ophthalmology review
explanation.pearls: Size the nasopharyngeal airway to reach from the nostril to the tragus and pass it about 1 cm beyond the tongue base; too short a tube fails to relieve the obstruction and is a common reason for apparent treatment failure.

sources.label: Australian Cleft Lip and Palate Association clinical resources

subtopic_detail: Treatment regimen for trichomoniasis diagnosed in the second trimester
stem:
You are the registrar in an antenatal clinic. A 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks in her second pregnancy describes 3 weeks of a frothy yellow-green discharge with vulval itch and soreness during sex. She has a single regular partner of 4 years.

She has taken no antibiotics recently and has not douched. She is not diabetic and her oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks is not yet due.

On speculum examination there is an adherent frothy discharge with punctate haemorrhages visible across the ectocervix, and the vaginal pH measures 5.5. A vaginal nucleic acid amplification test is positive for Trichomonas vaginalis and negative for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Her syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology from booking were both negative.

data_table.Examination: Adherent frothy vaginal discharge, punctate haemorrhages across the ectocervix, vaginal pH 5.5
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal nucleic acid amplification test positive for Trichomonas vaginalis, negative for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae; booking syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Tinidazole 2 g orally as a single dose for her, with the same dose given to her partner
options.rationale: Tinidazole is effective against Trichomonas vaginalis but Australian product information advises against its use in pregnancy because human safety data are far thinner than for metronidazole. It is the acceptable alternative outside pregnancy when metronidazole fails. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Clotrimazole 100 mg vaginal pessary at night for 6 nights, with no treatment for her partner
options.rationale: Clotrimazole treats candidiasis, which presents with a thick white discharge and a vaginal pH below 4.5 rather than the frothy discharge and pH of 5.5 here, and it has poor activity against Trichomonas vaginalis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Metronidazole 400 mg orally twice daily for 7 days, with the same course given to her partner
options.rationale: A 7-day oral metronidazole course is the preferred Australian regimen because cure rates exceed those of single-dose therapy, particularly in women with human immunodeficiency virus and in pregnancy, and metronidazole is regarded as safe in all trimesters. Concurrent partner treatment is essential since reinfection is otherwise the rule. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Metronidazole 2 g orally as a single dose for her, with the same dose given to her partner
options.rationale: Single-dose metronidazole is an accepted option where adherence is a concern, but randomised data show higher rates of treatment failure than the 7-day course, which is why the longer regimen is preferred. This is the near-pair worth distinguishing by cure rate rather than by safety. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Defer all antimicrobial therapy until after the birth, with a test of cure at 6 weeks postnatally
options.rationale: Deferring treatment leaves symptoms untreated and leaves the infection transmissible, and metronidazole has a long record of safe use across pregnancy including the first trimester. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmissible protozoal infection that is far more common in remote and regional Australian communities than in metropolitan populations, and nucleic acid amplification testing has largely replaced wet mount microscopy because its sensitivity is much higher. In pregnancy it is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight, although treatment has not been shown to reverse that risk, so the indication for treating is symptom relief and interruption of transmission. Metronidazole is the drug of choice in every trimester and while breastfeeding. Partner treatment without the need for the partner to be tested is standard, and patients should be advised to avoid sex until 7 days after both have completed therapy. A positive result should prompt a full sexually transmissible infection screen, since coinfection is common.
key_points: Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days is preferred over single-dose therapy because of higher cure rates
Metronidazole is safe in all trimesters of pregnancy and during breastfeeding
Treat partners empirically without waiting for their test results and advise no sex for 7 days after both finish
Tinidazole is a second-line alternative outside pregnancy, not a pregnancy option
A positive result should prompt screening for other sexually transmissible infections
explanation.pearls: Vaginal pH is the fastest bedside discriminator: candidiasis sits below 4.5, while trichomoniasis and bacterial vaginosis both run above 4.5, so a normal pH essentially excludes trichomoniasis.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Suppressive regimen for culture confirmed recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis
stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends your general practice frustrated by a fifth episode of vulval itch and a thick white discharge in the past 12 months. Each episode has settled with an over-the-counter antifungal cream and then returned within 6 to 8 weeks.

She uses condoms for contraception, has had the same partner for 6 years and has taken no antibiotics in the past year. She uses a plain soap-free wash and no vaginal products.

Her glycated haemoglobin is 5.2 per cent (below 6.0) and her human immunodeficiency virus serology is negative. A high vaginal swab taken during the current episode has grown Candida albicans on culture, with speciation confirmed and no resistance reported. On examination there is vulval erythema with fissuring in the natal cleft and a thick adherent white discharge. A pregnancy test is negative.

data_table.Examination: Vulval erythema with fissuring, thick adherent white vaginal discharge
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab culture positive for Candida albicans with no resistance reported, glycated haemoglobin 5.2% (below 6.0), human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fluconazole 150 mg orally on days 1, 4 and 7, then 150 mg weekly for 6 months
options.rationale: Four or more culture-proven episodes in a year defines recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, which is managed with an induction phase of three fluconazole doses 72 hours apart followed by weekly suppression for 6 months. Around 90 per cent of women remain free of symptoms while on suppression, although roughly half relapse after it stops. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

options.text: Fluconazole 150 mg orally as a single dose to be repeated with each further episode
options.rationale: Single-dose treatment of each episode is appropriate for sporadic candidiasis but does nothing to break the recurrence cycle, which is the actual problem once four or more episodes occur in a year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Boric acid 600 mg vaginal pessary at night for 14 nights, then review her symptoms
options.rationale: Boric acid is reserved for non-albicans species, particularly Candida glabrata, which is intrinsically less susceptible to fluconazole; the culture here confirms Candida albicans, for which azoles remain the right class. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

options.text: Nystatin vaginal pessary at night for 14 nights, then review her symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Nystatin is less effective than the azoles for vulvovaginal candidiasis and, like any single course, treats the current episode without addressing recurrence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Clotrimazole 100 mg vaginal pessary at night for 6 nights, repeated in the week before each period
options.rationale: Topical suppression timed to the menstrual cycle is a second-line option when oral therapy is contraindicated or refused, but oral fluconazole suppression has better evidence and much better adherence. (Source: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

explanation.summary: Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis is defined by four or more episodes in 12 months, and the diagnosis requires culture confirmation because up to half of women who self-treat for thrush have another cause such as dermatitis, lichen sclerosus or bacterial vaginosis. Speciation matters because Candida glabrata and Candida krusei respond poorly to fluconazole. The recognised contributors worth excluding are poorly controlled diabetes, immunosuppression, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics and high-dose oestrogen exposure. Management is a fluconazole induction phase followed by 6 months of weekly suppression, with counselling that relapse after cessation is common. Partner treatment is not indicated for candidiasis, which distinguishes it clearly from trichomoniasis.
key_points: Four or more culture-confirmed episodes in 12 months defines the recurrent form
Induction with three fluconazole doses 72 hours apart, then weekly suppression for 6 months
Speciate before treating, since Candida glabrata needs boric acid or nystatin rather than fluconazole
Exclude diabetes, immunosuppression and recent antibiotics as contributors
Partner treatment is not indicated, unlike in trichomoniasis
explanation.pearls: Fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy at any dose above a single 150 mg exposure, so pregnant women with recurrent disease are suppressed with topical clotrimazole instead; check the pregnancy test before writing a 6-month oral script.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Vaginal discharge and vulvovaginal candidiasis

subtopic_detail: Definitive drainage technique for a first presentation Bartholin abscess
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar on call. A 32-year-old woman presents with 4 days of increasing pain and swelling at the entrance to the vagina, now severe enough that she cannot sit down or walk comfortably.

She has never had a similar problem before. She is otherwise well, takes no regular medications, and has had no fever or rigors at home. Her last cervical screening test was 18 months ago and was negative for human papillomavirus.

On examination there is a tense, fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the posterior aspect of the introitus on the right, with overlying erythema but no spreading cellulitis into the labium or thigh. The swelling is exquisitely tender. There is no induration extending towards the ischiorectal fossa and no crepitus. Swabs have been taken for gonorrhoea and chlamydia nucleic acid amplification testing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 124/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.2 °C
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling at the right posterior introitus, overlying erythema without spreading cellulitis, no induration towards the ischiorectal fossa, no crepitus
data_table.Investigations: Nucleic acid amplification swabs for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral di-flucloxacillin with sitz baths and clinical review in 48 hours if no improvement
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone will not resolve a tense fluctuant collection, and the delay prolongs severe pain; antibiotics are added to drainage where there is surrounding cellulitis, immunosuppression or systemic illness. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Simple incision and drainage under local anaesthetic with a loose dressing and no catheter
options.rationale: Simple incision relieves pain immediately but the incision seals within days and recurrence rates are in the order of 10 to 15 per cent or higher, which is precisely the problem the Word catheter was designed to solve. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

options.text: Excision of the entire Bartholin gland under general anaesthetic on the next available list
options.rationale: Gland excision carries risks of significant bleeding from the underlying venous plexus, dyspareunia and scarring, and is reserved for repeated failure of simpler measures or where malignancy is suspected in a woman over 40. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

options.text: Incision and drainage with insertion of a Word catheter under local anaesthetic today
options.rationale: A Word catheter is left in for 4 to 6 weeks so that the tract epithelialises and a permanent drainage channel forms, which reduces recurrence compared with simple incision while remaining a bedside procedure under local anaesthetic. It is the first-line definitive treatment for a first presentation abscess. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Marsupialisation of the abscess cavity under general anaesthetic on the next available list
options.rationale: Marsupialisation is comparably effective at preventing recurrence but requires theatre and general anaesthesia, so it is generally kept for recurrence after a Word catheter rather than used first. (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management

explanation.summary: The Bartholin glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the vaginal introitus and drain through short ducts that can obstruct, producing a cyst that may then become infected. Most abscesses are polymicrobial with vaginal and enteric flora rather than being sexually transmitted, but gonorrhoea and chlamydia testing is still performed because they are recoverable in a minority. Definitive management aims to create a permanent drainage tract rather than simply emptying the cavity, which is why the Word catheter and marsupialisation outperform simple incision. A new Bartholin mass in a woman over 40 raises the possibility of a vulval or Bartholin gland carcinoma and warrants biopsy rather than blind drainage. Antibiotics are an adjunct, indicated for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, immunosuppression or pregnancy.
key_points: Word catheter insertion after incision creates an epithelialised tract and is first-line for a first abscess
The catheter stays in place for 4 to 6 weeks; simple incision alone recurs frequently
Marsupialisation and gland excision are escalation options, not first-line choices
Antibiotics are adjunctive and indicated for cellulitis, systemic illness, immunosuppression or pregnancy
A new Bartholin mass after age 40 requires biopsy to exclude carcinoma
explanation.pearls: Place the incision inside the hymenal ring on the mucosal surface rather than on the labial skin, since an external incision predisposes to a chronic draining fistula.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Bartholin cyst and abscess management
